grammarFocus: 转述动词；引述与改写；限定词 some / most / all 的范围。
title: The Campus Podcast: Reporting or Rumor?
instructions: 阅读下面的文章，回答10个问题。文章是一篇模拟的校园新闻报道，用于英语学习。请仔细阅读，注意转述动词和限定词（some / most / all）的用法。问题类型包括单选、填空、匹配和判断正误/未提及。填空答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制。所有解释均为中文。
passage:
Last month, the student newspaper at Greenfield University published an article about a new campus policy. The article claimed that the university planned to ban all student clubs from using the main hall for events. Within hours, the story spread across social media. Students reacted with anger and confusion. Some accused the administration of trying to silence student voices. Most students, however, simply wanted to know the facts.

The university's media office responded quickly. In a press release, a spokesperson stated that the newspaper had misunderstood the policy. She explained that the new rule only required clubs to book the hall two weeks in advance, not to stop using it. "We value student activities," she said. "This change is about organization, not restriction." The spokesperson also denied that the university had any plans to limit free speech on campus. She added that the university had always supported open discussion and would continue to do so.

A group of journalism students decided to investigate. They interviewed the newspaper's editor, a student named Maya Chen. Chen admitted that her team had not contacted the media office before publishing the story. "We relied on a document we found online," she said. "It was outdated, and we didn't check with the administration. That was our mistake." She added that the newspaper would publish a correction and apologize to readers. She also mentioned that the team had been under pressure to publish quickly and had skipped some steps.

The journalism students also spoke to club leaders. One leader, Jamal, told them that his club had already booked the hall for a concert. "The new rule is a bit annoying," he said, "but it's not a ban. We just have to plan ahead." Another leader, Sofia, agreed. She mentioned that most clubs had no problem with the two-week notice. "Some smaller clubs might struggle," she noted, "but the university has offered to help them with scheduling." Jamal added that he thought the newspaper should have asked the administration first.

The students then examined the original document that the newspaper had used. They found that it was a draft from three years ago, and it had never been approved. The current policy, available on the university website, clearly stated the two-week booking requirement. The students concluded that the newspaper had made an error by not verifying its source. They also noted that the document had been easy to find but had not been updated.

In their report, the journalism students wrote: "The initial story was based on incomplete information. While the newspaper did not intend to mislead, it failed to follow basic fact-checking procedures. We recommend that all student publications establish a clear verification process." The report was published on the journalism department's blog and shared widely. It included a checklist for reporters to use before publishing.

The newspaper's editor, Maya Chen, responded to the report. She wrote a public letter in which she acknowledged the mistake. "We were wrong to publish without checking," she wrote. "We have learned that speed is not more important than accuracy. We will do better." The university's media office accepted the apology and offered to hold a workshop on responsible reporting for all student journalists. The workshop was scheduled for the following month.

The incident sparked a campus-wide discussion about media literacy. Professors used the example in classes to teach students how to evaluate sources. Some students started a fact-checking club. Most students agreed that the experience, though embarrassing for the newspaper, had been a valuable lesson. As one student put it, "Now we know that not everything we read online is true, even if it's from a student newspaper." The university also announced that it would review its communication procedures to prevent similar misunderstandings in the future.

grammar.title: 转述动词与限定词的范围
grammar.explanation: 在英语中，转述动词（如 claim, state, explain, admit, deny, mention, note, recommend）用于引述他人的话或观点。不同的转述动词带有不同的含义，例如 claim 表示“声称”（可能不真实），admit 表示“承认”（通常指承认错误），deny 表示“否认”。此外，限定词 some, most, all 用于表示范围：some 表示“一些”（部分），most 表示“大多数”（大部分），all 表示“全部”。正确使用这些词可以使表达更准确。
grammar.example: Some accused the administration of trying to silence student voices. Most students, however, simply wanted to know the facts.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct word to complete the sentence: The teacher ______ that the exam would be difficult, but she did not say it was impossible.
options: admitted
claimed
mentioned
denied
questions.explanation: 这里只是提到考试会难，没有“承认错误”或“声称”的意味，因此用 mentioned 最合适。

questions.prompt: Choose the correct word to complete the sentence: The company ______ that it had broken the law and agreed to pay a fine.
options: denied
admitted
claimed
explained
questions.explanation: 公司承认违法并同意支付罚款，因此用 admitted（承认）。

questions.prompt: Choose the correct word to complete the sentence: ______ of the students in the class passed the test, but a few failed.
options: All
Most
Some
None
questions.explanation: 句子说“但有几个没通过”，说明大部分通过了，因此用 Most（大多数）。

questions.prompt: Choose the correct word to complete the sentence: The politician ______ that he had received money from the company, but later evidence proved he had.
options: admitted
denied
mentioned
explained
questions.explanation: 后半句说“但后来的证据证明他收了钱”，说明他之前否认了，因此用 denied（否认）。
